how-to-discipline-a-child-without-shouti:
Discipline and punishment have become near-synonyms, which is a shame, because the word means something more useful than it is usually used for. To discipline is to teach. Everything below follows from that: if a child has not learned anything, the discipline has not worked, however unpleasant it was.

A child who is flooded cannot learn

This is the piece of biology that decides most of the rest. When a child is in full distress (furious, frightened, humiliated) the parts of the brain that hold reasoning and impulse control are least available. Lecturing at that moment is not merely ineffective; it is asking for a capacity that is temporarily offline.

So the order is: settle, then teach. Not settle instead of teaching, which is where this idea usually goes wrong. The teaching still happens. It happens ten minutes later, briefly, when there is somebody there to hear it.

If the lesson has to be delivered at volume to land, it is not landing. It is being survived.

What works instead of escalation

  • Say less. A sentence lands; a lecture does not. "Hitting stops the game" carries more than three minutes of explanation about why we do not hit.
  • Consequences that belong to the act. Paint on the table gets wiped up by the person who spilt it. A bike ridden into the road comes inside for the afternoon. These teach because the link is visible; an unrelated punishment teaches only that adults can impose costs.
  • Repair, not just apology. A forced sorry teaches the word. Rebuilding the knocked-over tower, or fetching the ice pack, teaches what the word is for.
  • Follow through quietly the first time. The reason households escalate is that the first request has no weight. Weight comes from something reliably happening, not from volume.
  • Teach the replacement. "Don't grab" leaves a child with nothing to do instead. "Ask, and if they say no, come and find me" gives them a move they can actually make.

What about consequences that are meant to sting?

They change behaviour in the short term. That is why they persist. What the evidence does not support is that they teach the thing parents want taught. A child who has been punished has learned mainly to avoid the punishment, which often means becoming better at not being caught rather than better at not doing it.

The more useful test is simple: after this, does my child know what to do differently? If the answer is no, whatever just happened was not discipline.

The part that is genuinely hard

This approach asks more of the adult than shouting does. It requires you to be steadier than the child at the exact moment they are least steady, and to come back to a subject later when the moment has passed and it would be easier to let it go. That is real work, and it is why it is worth arranging your week so that you are not doing it on four hours of sleep.

The measure of discipline is not whether the behaviour stopped today. It is whether the child is better equipped next time.
how-to-handle-a-stubborn-child:
The child described as stubborn is very often a child who has worked out that almost nothing in their day is theirs to decide, and has located the few places where they still have a say. Meals, clothes, hair, bedtime, the coat. Those are not random battlegrounds. They are the places where a small person can still exercise a will.

What stubbornness usually is

Between roughly two and four, and again in early adolescence, children go through periods where asserting a separate will is the developmental work itself. It is not a flaw to be corrected out of them; it is the beginning of a person who can say no to things later, which is a capacity most parents very much want their teenager to have.

That reframing is not merely comforting. It changes the tactics, because the goal stops being "win" and becomes "give the will somewhere legitimate to go".

A child with no say anywhere will find a place to have one. It is usually the least convenient place available.

Give ground where it costs nothing

  • Two acceptable options, not an open question. "The red coat or the blue one" hands over a real decision while keeping the coat non-negotiable. "Do you want to put your coat on?" hands over the coat.
  • Let the small things be theirs. Mismatched socks, an odd choice of jumper, the order they eat things in. Every one of these is a place a child gets to be a person, and none of them matter.
  • Separate what is genuinely fixed. Safety, kindness, and a handful of household necessities. Everything else is potentially negotiable, and knowing which is which stops you defending a hill you did not mean to be on.
  • Give time, not just instruction. Much of what looks like refusal is a child who needs ninety seconds to finish the thing in their head. A warning before a transition removes an enormous amount of apparent stubbornness.

When you cannot give ground

Some things are not negotiable, and the answer is to be immovable and warm at once. State it once. Do not argue it. Acknowledge how annoying it is. Then hold.

"We are holding hands across the car park. I know you hate it. It is not up for discussion today."

The temptation is to explain more, hoping that a good enough reason will produce agreement. It will not, and each extra explanation reads as an opening for further negotiation.

The temperament question

Some children are simply more determined than others, from very early on, and that does not change much across childhood. If that is your child, the goal is not to sand it off. Determination is a genuine asset later. It is the same trait that keeps somebody at a difficult task, or refusing a bad idea from a friend at fourteen. The work is to help them aim it, not to break it.

A child who never pushes back is not necessarily easier to raise. They are just easier this year.
why-does-my-child-not-listen-to-me:
There are four ordinary reasons a child does not do what they were asked, and only one of them is defiance. Most parents work through them in the wrong order. Starting with the assumption of disrespect and arriving last at the explanation that is usually correct.

One: they did not receive it

Instructions delivered across a room, over noise, or to the back of a head are frequently not registered as instructions at all. A child absorbed in something has a genuinely narrowed attention. That focus is a good thing, and it is the same capacity you want them to have over homework in six years.

The test is unglamorous: go to them, get to their eye level, wait until they look at you. If compliance improves immediately, the problem was never listening.

Two: it was too much to hold

Working memory, how much a child can keep in mind while doing something with it, is still developing well into adolescence. A four-part instruction to a six-year-old routinely arrives as one and a half parts.

The child who goes upstairs and comes back with nothing is not being obtuse. They genuinely no longer have the list.

Before deciding a child will not, it is worth ruling out that they cannot, and cannot is far commoner than it looks.

Three: they cannot switch yet

Stopping an absorbing activity to start a dull one is a specific skill, harder than either activity. It relies on the same slow-maturing control system as impulse and planning. This is why the same child obeys instantly at the door and appears deaf at the table.

A warning before the switch, "two more turns", does more than any amount of firmness at the moment of the switch itself.

Four: the first ask does not mean anything

This is the uncomfortable one, and it is a household design problem rather than a child problem. If requests one through three are routinely followed by requests four and five, and nothing happens until a voice rises, then the child has accurately learned the system. They are not ignoring the rule. They have identified it.

The repair is not volume. It is asking once, then going and making the thing happen (a hand on the shoulder, a walk to the sink), so that the first request reliably has something behind it.

What about actual defiance?

It exists, and it is worth taking seriously when it is genuinely what is happening: a child who has heard, understood, is capable, and refuses. Even then, the useful question is what the refusal is for. It is usually about autonomy, fairness between siblings, or something that happened earlier in the day that nobody has mentioned.

Persistent, escalating refusal across settings, home and school both, over months rather than weeks is worth raising with somebody who can observe your child directly. That is a different conversation from the ordinary not-listening this piece is about.

Work through the four in order. Most families find their answer before they reach the fourth.
how-to-stay-calm-when-your-child-is-havi:
Staying calm during a tantrum is treated as a personality trait. Some parents have it, some do not. It is closer to a physical skill, and like other physical skills it can be prepared for in advance and practised. What it cannot be is summoned by deciding to be a calmer person in the middle of the noise.

What is happening to you

A child in full distress is loud, unpredictable and often aimed at you. Your body responds the way bodies do: heart rate up, breathing shallow, muscles tight, attention narrowed. That is a threat response, and it happens before any thought about parenting philosophy arrives.

This matters because it explains why good intentions fail. You are not losing an argument with yourself about patience. You are trying to think clearly in a body that has already prepared for a fight.

You cannot reason your way to calm from inside a stress response. You have to come down through the body first.

What to do with your own body, in order

  • Breathe out longer than you breathe in. Four in, six or eight out. The long out-breath is the part that shifts the nervous system; the deep in-breath on its own does very little.
  • Get lower. Sit, crouch, or lean on something. Standing over a screaming child keeps your body in a posture of confrontation and keeps them in one of threat.
  • Unclench something. Hands, jaw, shoulders. Choose one and let it go deliberately.
  • Stop talking. You do not need to say anything at all for the first minute, and most of what people say in that minute makes it longer.

What to do about the child

Less than you think. A tantrum is not a negotiation and it is not usually a behaviour to be corrected while it is happening. It is a nervous system past its limit. The job is safety and presence, not resolution.

  • Make it safe. Move sharp things, move them off the road, stay near.
  • Stay, quietly. Nearby, unhurried, not looming and not leaving. Presence does more than words.
  • Do not teach yet. The lesson lands afterwards, briefly. Delivered mid-tantrum it is not heard, and it extends the episode.
  • Do not move the limit. Giving in mid-tantrum resolves this one and makes the next one longer, because it demonstrates what the tantrum is for.

Prepare in advance

Most of the difficulty is decided before the tantrum starts. Your capacity to stay steady drops sharply when you are tired, hungry, late or already frayed, the same mechanism that makes your child less able to cope. Households where tantrums go better are usually not calmer by temperament; they have simply arranged the day so the flashpoints are not stacked.

It also helps to have decided in advance what you will do, so that you are executing a plan rather than making a decision while somebody screams.

Afterwards

Once they are settled, keep it short. A brief naming of what happened, a repair if something needs repairing, and then genuinely move on. Long post-mortems teach a child that a tantrum buys an hour of intense parental attention, which is not the lesson intended.

And if you did not stay calm: say so plainly, keep the limit, and let it go. A parent who loses their temper occasionally and repairs it is doing something children handle perfectly well.

Your calm is not a mood you have to find. It is a set of things you do with your body while you wait.
